summary: This strategic plan outlines a comprehensive roadmap for scaling neutral atom quantum computers from current thousands of qubits toward 10,000–100,000 physical qubits required for practical quantum advantage, integrating advances in hardware, photonic control, error correction, and circuit compilation. The plan emphasizes that neutral atoms have demonstrated below-threshold error correction, two-qubit gate fidelities exceeding 99.5%, and dynamically reconfigurable connectivity, positioning the platform to achieve megaquop-scale computations within the next decade.
motivation: Neutral atom arrays have matured significantly, recently achieving the first below-threshold error correction demonstration with gate fidelities above 99.5%, making practical quantum advantage attainable. However, substantial challenges remain in scaling system size, controlling increasing numbers of qubits, and reducing cycle times for error correction, requiring coordinated theoretical and experimental advances.
method: The plan identifies research directions across seven major areas: (1) defining and verifying practical quantum advantage with 10³–10¹² quops, (2) scaling qubit arrays to 10,000–100,000 atoms via higher laser power and optical lattices, (3) developing scalable integrated photonic control with silicon nitride and lithium niobate platforms, (4) implementing quantum error correction with high-rate qLDPC codes and improved decoders, (5) optimizing quantum circuit compilation for reconfigurable architectures, and (6) networking multiple QPUs through cavity-enhanced atom-photon entanglement and transportable arrays.
result: Physical qubit counts have grown at ~1.8× per year while gate errors decreased by ~0.6× per year; recent demonstrations achieved distance-5 surface codes operating >2× below threshold with atom-loss detection. At current scaling rates, neutral atoms could reach utility-scale computation within the next decade, though this depends critically on closing the gap between current demonstrations (hundreds of logical qubits, MHz-level clock cycles) and practical requirements (>10⁶ quops, microsecond-scale readout).
